subject: chemistry
question_text: Name the element with the highest electron affinity (E.A) and the element with the highest electronegativity (E.N) in the periodic table.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question
Classification of Elements – Periodic Properties · 2 marks

steps.label: Highest electron affinity
lines: It is chlorine and not fluorine: in fluorine's
small 2p subshell the incoming electron is
strongly repelled, so fluorine releases less
steps.why: The expected answer by the general trend would be fluorine, so the one-line reason for chlorine shows the exception is understood, not guessed.
common_mistakes: Writing fluorine. The repulsion inside fluorine's small 2p subshell makes chlorine the element that releases the most energy.
Naming a group instead of an element. The question asks for one element.
steps.memory_tip: Electron affinity peaks one row down from fluorine: chlorine.
steps.margin_note: This pairs with the question on E.A of chlorine versus fluorine; the same reason works in both.

steps.label: Highest electronegativity

lines.text: Highest E.A: Cl — Highest E.N: F

lines: It is the smallest and most strongly
steps.why: Electronegativity measures the pull of a bonded atom on the shared pair. No incoming electron is being added, so fluorine's small size only strengthens the pull and fluorine has the highest value. The word smallest in the answer line is a comparison among the atoms that attract a shared pair strongly: fluorine is the smallest of those. Hydrogen and helium have smaller atomic radii, but they are not strong attractors of a shared pair.
common_mistakes: Writing fluorine for both quantities. Fluorine is the trend-expected answer, but electron affinity peaks at chlorine.
Giving electronegativity units. It is a relative number with no units.
steps.memory_tip: Two different questions: taking in a free electron favours Cl; pulling a shared pair favours F.
steps.margin_note: The value 4.0 is worth writing; it marks fluorine as the scale's top.

insider_note: The common error is writing fluorine for both — electron affinity peaks at chlorine while electronegativity peaks at fluorine, and this question exists to test exactly that split.
